content: 1. The study by Yassin et al. demonstrated that innovative community-based approaches in Southern Ethiopia led to a doubling of tuberculosis (TB) case notifications and improved treatment outcomes. (PLOS ONE, 2015) 2. Zachariah et al. compared passive and active TB case finding and the use of isoniazid preventive therapy among household contacts in a rural district of Malawi, highlighting the benefits of active case finding. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2003) 3. Ketema et al. evaluated the integration of TB screening and contact investigation in Ethiopian TB clinics using a mixed-methods study, emphasizing the importance of systematic approaches. (PLOS ONE, 2021) 4. The WHO consolidated guidelines on TB management in children and adolescents (Module 5) provide comprehensive recommendations for managing TB in these populations, including diagnostic and treatment strategies. (WHO, 2021) 5. Miyano et al. explored the association between TB treatment outcomes and a mobile antiretroviral therapy program in Zambia, demonstrating improved outcomes with integrated care. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2013) 6. Wingfield et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial in Peru, showing that socioeconomic support significantly enhanced TB prevention and treatment outcomes. (Bull World Health Organ, 2017) 7. Rocha et al. assessed the Innovative Socio-economic Interventions Against Tuberculosis (ISIAT) project, which aimed to address TB through operational and socioeconomic strategies. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis, 2011) 8. The WHO guidelines on latent TB infection provide updated recommendations for programmatic management, emphasizing systematic screening and preventive treatment. (WHO, 2021) 9. The WHO policy on collaborative TB/HIV activities outlines guidelines for national programs to address the dual burden of TB and HIV, including routine HIV testing for TB patients. (WHO, 2012) 10. The WHO consolidated guidelines on TB prevention (Module 1) recommend the use of tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for TB infection testing, with strong recommendations against replacing TST with IGRAs in lowand middle-income countries. (WHO, 2020) 11. The WHO guidelines on TB diagnosis (Module 3) recommend the use of Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra as initial diagnostic tests for TB and rifampicin resistance in children and adults, particularly in cases of pulmonary TB, extrapulmonary TB, and TB meningitis. (WHO, 2021) 12. The WHO guidelines on TB treatment (Module 4) provide updated recommendations for drug-susceptible and drug-resistant TB treatment, including specific dosing regimens for children. (WHO, 2022) 13. The WHO guidelines on nutritional care for TB patients emphasize the importance of addressing malnutrition as part of comprehensive TB care. (WHO, 2013) 14. The WHO guidelines on the management of severe acute malnutrition in children provide updated recommendations for integrating nutritional support into TB care. (WHO, 2013) 15. The WHO operational handbook on TB management in children and adolescents includes detailed dosing recommendations for TB medications, such as isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, tailored to pediatric needs. (WHO, 2014) 16. The WHO guidelines strongly recommend against the use of commercial serodiagnostic tests for diagnosing active pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB in children, regardless of HIV status, due to very low-quality evidence supporting their use. (WHO, 2011) 17. Routine HIV testing should be offered to all patients, including children, with presumptive or diagnosed TB, as part of collaborative TB/HIV activities. (WHO, 2012) 18. The WHO guidelines recommend the use of Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra for diagnosing TB meningitis in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimens, given the urgency of rapid diagnosis. (WHO, 2021) 19. The WHO guidelines emphasize that Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra should be used for detecting rifampicin resistance in extrapulmonary TB specimens, such as lymph node aspirates, pleural fluid, and urine, rather than conventional methods. (WHO, 2021) 20. The WHO guidelines recommend against replacing TST with IGRAs in lowand middle-income countries for diagnosing TB infection in children, due to low-quality evidence. (WHO, 2020)
